title: Ivo and the Vow
premise: Felix Eastwick inherited his family's failing vineyard along with its crushing debts, and the only lifeline is a prestigious harvest festival grant that requires him to complete an anonymous pen-pal mentorship with a rival winemaker. His assigned correspondent turns out to be Marguerite Voss, the sharp-tongued consultant hired by the bank to decide whether Eastwick Vineyards deserves to survive—and neither realizes who they're writing to until feelings have already taken root. As their anonymous letters deepen into intimacy while their daytime rivalry sharpens, Felix must choose between concealing his identity to protect the vineyard and confessing everything before the festival's final toast. He chooses truth, risking both the grant and her career, and Marguerite—forced to choose between the bank that made her and the man who unmade her armor—resigns, buys a stake in the vineyard with him, and stays.
about_author: Theo Brightwater is the pen name of a former sommelier who spent a decade pouring wine in coastal towns before turning to writing full-time. Their novels are known for slow-burn romance set against working landscapes, where love is earned as honestly as a harvest.

chapters.title: Debts Instead of Grapes
chapters.summary: Felix's POV. Three years after inheriting Eastwick Vineyards, Felix surveys frost-damaged rows and a stack of overdue notices, then receives word he's been accepted into the Harvest Festival grant program—with one condition: a season-long anonymous correspondence with an industry mentor. The beat is weary hope: one last chance disguised as homework.

chapters.title: The Bank Sends Its Knife
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. Marguerite Voss arrives in town representing Meridian Bank, tasked with evaluating whether Eastwick Vineyards is worth restructuring or repossessing. She meets Felix at a tense first inspection where his pride and her precision clash immediately. The beat is mutual misjudgment: each decides the other is exactly what they appear to be.

chapters.title: First Letter, Unsigned
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. Both write their opening letters through the festival program's anonymized portal—Felix honest for once because no one knows it's him; Marguerite surprisingly candid because the rules forbid professional talk. The beat is accidental intimacy: two people who can't stand each other by day begin telling the truth by night.

chapters.title: Pruning Season
chapters.summary: Felix's POV. Marguerite's daylight audit begins in earnest—she questions every expense, and Felix bristles at being treated like a liability. But her offhand advice about canopy management is genuinely good, and he grudgingly uses it. The beat is reluctant respect taking root beneath open hostility.

chapters.title: What I'd Never Say Aloud
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. In her third letter, Marguerite admits she gave up making wine herself years ago for a stable corporate path, something she's never confessed to anyone. Reading it, Felix feels seen in a way that unsettles him. The beat is vulnerability exchanged under cover of anonymity.

chapters.title: The Town Talks
chapters.summary: Felix's POV. At the weekly market, gossip links the mysterious bank consultant to the festival program, and Felix jokes with his cellar hand Dario about what he'd say if his pen-pal turned out to be 'that viper.' Meanwhile Marguerite watches him defend her anonymously without knowing it. The beat is dramatic irony tightening its grip.

chapters.title: Rain on the Trellis
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. A storm forces Felix and Marguerite to shelter together in the cellar overnight, and stripped of audiences, they talk until dawn—about grief, ambition, the families that shaped them. It's the closest they've come, and both retreat hard the next morning. The beat is connection followed by panic.

chapters.title: A Letter Too Close to Home
chapters.summary: Felix's POV. His pen-pal describes a childhood memory of a stone farmhouse with blue shutters—the exact description of Eastwick's neighboring property where Marguerite grew up. Felix dismisses the coincidence, but unease plants itself. The beat is suspicion denied: the reader sees it, he refuses to.

chapters.title: The Grant Committee
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. The festival committee reveals that the bank's evaluation will directly influence the grant decision, putting Marguerite in a conflict of interest she must hide. Her letter that week grows guarded, and Felix notices the distance. The beat is duty beginning to corrupt honesty on both sides.

chapters.title: Harvest Hands
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. Harvest begins, and Marguerite—against protocol—works a day in the fields beside Felix. Sweat and laughter erode the rivalry; Dario teases them mercilessly. That night both write letters describing the same day without naming each other. The beat is joy that neither can reconcile with their positions.

chapters.title: What the Numbers Say
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. Marguerite finishes her report: Eastwick Vineyards is not viable without the grant, and her recommendation could kill it. She drafts a favorable addendum she has no authority to make, then deletes it. The beat is power's corruption pressing on conscience from both directions.

chapters.title: The Almost-Confession
chapters.summary: Felix's POV. On the eve of the festival, Felix nearly tells Marguerite he's her pen-pal—he's pieced it together—but she preempts him with cold professionalism, having learned the committee suspects her objectivity. Wounded, he says something cruel instead. The beat is love weaponized into retreat.

chapters.title: Letters Unsent
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. Marguerite writes a letter admitting she knows her pen-pal is Felix and that she's fallen for both versions of him—then burns it rather than compromise them both. Felix, meanwhile, writes his own confession and can't bring himself to send it. The beat is parallel cowardice, tender and maddening.

chapters.title: Festival Eve
chapters.summary: Felix's POV. The town fills with visitors, string lights, and rival vintners. Felix learns the bank plans to announce repossession immediately after the festival regardless of the grant—a leak meant to bury Eastwick. The beat is the floor giving way: even winning may no longer be enough.

chapters.title: The Anonymous Toast
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. At the festival's opening gala, the program reveals pen-pal identities in a public ceremony. Names are called; Felix and Marguerite stand across the room from each other as the truth lands on the whole crowd at once. The beat is exposure: the private thing made suddenly, brutally public.

chapters.title: Accusations
chapters.summary: Felix's POV. Feeling manipulated—she knew his finances all along, he argues—Felix accuses Marguerite of running a con. She counters that he courted her under false pretenses too. Dario and the townsfolk watch the fracture. The beat is both of them right and both of them wrong, saying unforgivable things.

chapters.title: Meridian Makes Its Offer
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. The bank offers Marguerite a promotion if she delivers the repossession recommendation personally; refusing means her resignation and likely blacklisting in the industry. She walks the vineyard alone at night, remembering the cellar conversation. The beat is the choice crystallizing: career or truth.

chapters.title: The Last Letter
chapters.summary: Felix's POV. Felix writes one final letter through the now-defunct portal, knowing it goes nowhere, laying out everything: the debts, the fear, the way her letters saved him before he ever liked her. Dario quietly submits it to the festival's closing reading instead. The beat is surrender to sincerity.

chapters.title: Read Aloud
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. At the festival's closing ceremony, Felix's letter is read to the crowd before the final toast. Marguerite listens in front of everyone, including her bank superiors, and understands what staying invisible cost them both. The beat is public reckoning—humiliation transmuted into clarity.

chapters.title: The Choice Before the Toast
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. With the final toast minutes away, Marguerite takes the stage and announces her resignation from Meridian, declaring Eastwick Vineyards viable and herself its new partner-in-evaluation-turned-partner-in-fact. Felix, stunned, must respond publicly. The beat is climax: love declared against duty, with consequences pending.

chapters.title: After the Applause
chapters.summary: Felix's POV. The grant is awarded, but the bank retaliates—calling the loan due early. Marguerite's savings, Felix's land, and Dario's faith pool together into a restructuring plan built on the festival's momentum and pre-orders. The beat is aftermath with teeth: victory that must still be paid for.

chapters.title: Vow
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. One year later, at the next harvest festival, Felix and Marguerite pour their first joint vintage—named for the vow they made in letters before they ever trusted each other in person. Surrounded by found family and honest work, they sign their names side by side. The beat is resolution: love chosen in daylight, at last.
